KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Reply to Applicants’ Response to Appeal                                                Page 2 of 21
          Pro se intervenor Kevin Kennedy (“Mr. Kennedy”) files this reply to the response of

Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Services

Corporation (“LCRA TSC”) (collectively, “Applicants”) to Mr. Kennedy’s Appeal of SOAH

Order No. 35 and Request for Commission-Directed Independent Technical Investigation and

Forensic Audit (the “Appeal”) of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (“ERCOT”) modeling

used in the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”). 1


        Applicants filed their Response on September 30, 2026, and Mr. Kennedy received it the

same day. This reply is filed within five working days of receipt and is timely under 16 Tex.

Admin. Code (“TAC”) § 22.78(a). Because the Appeal remains pending before the Commission

under 16 TAC § 22.123(a)(6) and (7), Mr. Kennedy respectfully asks that the Commission

consider this reply together with the Appeal.



                                           I.     INTRODUCTION

        Mr. Kennedy is a pro se intervenor; he is not a lawyer. He is a directly affected

landowner. He is a retired professional engineer who was licensed to practice engineering in

Texas for over 30 years. Mr. Kennedy previously owned and led a highly respected

transportation consulting firm for almost 20 years. Mr. Kennedy’s firm provided planning and

design services to TxDOT on major projects statewide. That work involved complex travel

demand and three-dimensional hydraulic modeling to predict future conditions based on forecast

inputs and network flow/transfer capabilities.




1
 Applicants’ Response to Kevin Kennedy’s Appeal of SOAH Order No. 35 (Sept. 30, 2026) (Item No. 6610)
(“Applicants’ Response”); Kevin Kennedy’s Appeal of SOAH Order No. 35 and Request for Commission-Directed
Independent Technical Investigation and Forensic Audit (Sept. 23, 2026) (Item No. 6601 in Docket No. 59475; Item
No. 619 in Docket No. 59182).

          There are many engineering parallels between cars flowing through a roadway network,

water flowing through a drainage network, and electricity flowing through a transmission

network. The paramount need for complete and accurate input data is equaled only by the need

for the full interconnected network to be properly modeled. Even if a study’s purpose is focused

on a particular sub-region within the network, the conditions in a sub-region are not isolated

from or immune to changing conditions in the remainder of an interconnected network.

         That is the situation we have here. The PBRP may have focused on the Permian Basin,

but its findings and recommendations relied on ERCOT’s system-wide model. If the system-

wide model input was incomplete or inaccurate, the results generated by the model would also be

inaccurate. To disregard known, dramatic changes to load demand input variables and generation

supply necessary to balance that load, in significant portions of the model, would invalidate

model output. ERCOT failed to add new HB 5066 load demand in about 80% of the model.

                          II.     THE APPEAL IS PROCEDURALLY PROPER

         The purpose of the Appeal was to make the Commission aware that the ERCOT

modeling that serves as the foundation of the PBRP recommendations, and more specifically

Import Path 2, is likely flawed and must be audited via an independent technical investigation.

The Appeal sought to point out that there is substantial, credible, and compelling evidence that

ERCOT’s model did not properly consider all HB 5066 TSP loads and therefore the import path

power flow transfer recommendations are not valid or reliable. The Appeal also sought to remind

the Commission that it has both the authority and obligation to audit ERCOT operations and

investigate this apparent modeling flaw2, now that it has been so clearly and publicly brought to

 their attention. Mr. Kennedy believed, and continues to believe, his motion to the SOAH ALJs

was the proper course of action to initiate this notification and request for audit.

        The Applicants’ Response seems to try to gloss over the State Office of Administrative

Hearing’s (“SOAH’s”) jurisdictional limitations. The Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) in

SOAH Order 35 were not saying that Mr. Kennedy was substantively wrong on the law. They

never reached that conclusion because they determined that they did not have authority to make

the decision in the first place. That is, the ALJs lacked jurisdiction because the Public Utility

Commission (“Commission”) or statutes never gave them that authority. Therefore, Mr.

Kennedy’s question to them was only improper in the sense that SOAH lacked proper

jurisdiction. The ALJs, in fact, clarified the issue by stating that the Commission has sole

authority over Mr. Kennedy’s request. 3

        Mr. Kennedy argues that under the doctrine of exhaustion of administrative remedies had

he raised his request for an audit first with the Commission, the Applicants might well have

attempted to argue that he should have initiated that request at SOAH. The approach taken by

Mr. Kennedy assures that the record reflects that the ALJs deferred to the Commission on the

substantive merits of his request. Mr. Kennedy has perfectly complied with 16 TAC § 22.123 in

a situation where the ALJs assert that they lack jurisdiction to rule.


        Applicants’ lead argument is that the Appeal fails 16 TAC § 22.123(a)(3) because Mr.

Kennedy agrees with the ALJs about the limits of SOAH’s power. 4 That argument misreads the

rule. Section 22.123(a)(1) makes an appeal available for any interim order that “immediately

prejudices a substantial or material right of a party or materially affects the course of the

proceeding.” Section 22.123(a)(3) requires the appeal to “specify the reasons why the interim

of a party or materially affects the course of the proceeding.” Nothing in the rule limits

“improper” to a legal error by the presiding officer. An order can be right about the limits of

SOAH’s own power and still be improper as a disposition, because it ends the inquiry instead of

sending it to the only body that can act.


        That is what happened here. The ALJs held that SOAH lacks investigative power and that

the Commission “has complete oversight and exclusive jurisdiction over ERCOT.” 5 Having said

so, the ALJs could have certified the question to the Commission under 16 TAC § 22.127, which

allows a presiding officer to certify, on his or her own motion, issues concerning “which rules or

statutes are applicable to a proceeding” and “whether commission policy should be established

or clarified as to a substantive or procedural issue of significance to the proceeding.” 6 They

instead denied the motion outright. A request that only the Commission can make would then

never reach the Commission at all unless Mr. Kennedy appealed. An appeal under § 22.123 was

the only door left open, and the rule does not require a party to pretend the ALJs misread the law

in order to walk through it.


        The order also “materially affects the course of the proceeding.” On September 18, 2026,

the Commission remanded this case to SOAH on Preliminary Order Issue No. 11: “Are the

proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards?” 7 The

PBRP is the reliability study on which Applicants rest their answer to that question. In the same

order that denied Mr. Kennedy’s motion, the ALJs ruled that they “will not reopen the

evidentiary record.”8 The underlying ERCOT modeling data that Mr. Kennedy sought through

requirement of PURA § 39.151.”13 Great weight is not blind weight. The more weight the

           Lastly, whether there may have been a better or more palatable avenue to notify the

Commission of the flawed model, it is immaterial at this point; the Commission is aware and

now must act in the public’s interest. The fire department cannot refuse to respond to a fire just

because someone drove to the fire station and told them about the fire directly, rather than the

fire department’s preferred method of receiving a 911 call. It would now be an unconscionable

act if the Commission were to ignore the significant evidence of an invalid PBRP model.


           III.    THE APPLICANTS DO NOT APPEAR TO UNDERSTAND MODELING

           The Applicants assert “the technical premises underlying Mr. Kennedy’s Appeal are

factually inaccurate” and “rest on a fundamental misunderstanding of the differences between

the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”) and the 2024 Regional Transmission Plan (“2024

RTP”).” 14 In fact, the opposite is true.

           Either the authors of the Applicants’ response do not appear to have a clear grasp of

engineering and basic modeling, or maybe they are hoping the Commission does not. The

Commission must see through the Applicants’ flimsy attempt to conflate the modeling needs of a

supposed small project study with the necessary modeling requirements of a regional study that

also recommends multiple long-haul, import paths stretching the width of the ERCOT system,

drawing from generation supply resources from the far corners of that same ERCOT system.

         The Applicants have established in the evidentiary record that they did not develop the

load cases or perform the studies, and they do not have the load demand data and future/

proposed generation data beyond what is provided in the PBRP report, yet they try mightily to

convince the Commission that Mr. Kennedy’s assertions of a potentially flawed model “should

be rejected”, even though they present no evidence to contradict Mr. Kennedy’s substantial and

compelling evidence that the model is likely invalid and should be audited.

        Further, the Applicants’ modeling expert, Jared Gurley, confirms Mr. Kennedy’s finding

that, based off of the study reports, “all of the cases used in all of the studies contained the entire

ERCOT system.” 18

        The question the Commission must decide is whether it is generally accepted engineering

practice to utilize a questionable inter-connected system model, that ignores substantial portions

of known load demand, on a far-reaching study like the PBRP, as the Applicants assert, or, as

Mr. Kennedy has established, sound engineering judgment would require a model built with all

known forecasted load, with all necessary balancing generation included.

        The 2024-RTP includes 59,200-MW 19 of added future generation need to offset

forecasted load demand, while the PBRP includes only 17,170-MW 20 of added future

generation. This yields a difference in forecasted load demand of about 42,000-MW between the

two concurrent ERCOT system models. It is unlikely that any reasonable engineer would assert

you can leave 42,000-MW of known forecasted load demand out of the PBRP system flow

model, representing an almost 40% omission, and it will not affect the power transfer results for

multiple 400-mile bulk transfer import paths. If the ERCOT engineer in responsible charge

believes the models are consistent, ask them to write a technical memorandum, made available to

        The answer is as obvious as it is inescapable: ERCOT’s PBRP modeling must be

        examined a 2038 planning horizon. The 2024 RTP, by contrast, was a system-
        wide planning assessment for the 2030 planning horizon. In other words, one
        study examined regional reliability considerations while the other study evaluated
        how those considerations fit within the broader needs of the ERCOT electric
        system. The two studies served fundamentally different purposes and, as a result,
        appropriately used different inputs and assumptions.”23

        These statements provide further evidence that the Applicants do not appear to

comprehend how the flow model of an interconnect system functions.

       First, the PBRP and 2024-RTP were developed contemporaneously, beginning with the

same 2023-RTP model as their starting point. They each had the same universe of system-wide

future load demand and generation supply forecasts to draw from. They both modeled 2030

planning horizons, which should have been represented in the modeling as ERCOT’s best and

most reliable set of assumptions of future conditions. The future supply and demand inputs in the

two 2030 models should have matched, but they did not. For currently unknown reasons,

ERCOT chose to disregard approximately 80% of the known future load forecasts in their PBRP

model. This amounted to an approximate 42,000-MW difference in both future load demand and

offsetting future generation supply between ERCOT’s PBRP model input and their simultaneous

2024-RTP model input. It is unlikely any reasonable engineer would claim such an omission

would not have a potentially significant effect on modeled power flows.

       Second, the dramatic 42,000-MW difference in the magnitude of generation supply and

load demand model inputs, coupled with the significant difference in the geographic or spatial

placement of both supply and demand inputs render the two models unique and contradictory.

The power flow patterns resulting from the temporal and spatial differences in supply and

demand, would be significantly different, though the goal of the modeling should have been the

same: model the anticipated future conditions as accurately and consistently as reasonable so that

there is a high degree of confidence in the necessary transmission improvements identified by the

modeling. There is no obvious reasonable or excusable engineering explanation to create two

entirely different models, using a mix of old and new load demands, if attempting to predict the

same 2030 conditions. Per ERCOT has a responsibility to make their best effort to create models

that accurately reflect anticipated future conditions. ERCOT must be required to explain the

major discrepancies between two simultaneously developed 2030 models.

KENNEDY 59182 & 59475 – Reply to Applicants’ Response to Appeal                       Page 13 of 21
         Notably, Applicants do not dispute the numbers. They concede that the PBRP case added

only “approximately 17,170 MW” of new generation, and that the 2024 RTP “contained

materially more new statewide load and associated generation than the PBRP case.”24

Applicants also concede that load outside West Texas in the PBRP “was based on the 2023 RTP

load data.”25 Their only answer is that the two studies had different purposes. Different purposes

do not change the laws of physics. Power flowing on a 765-kV import path depends on where the

load and generation are actually located within the interconnected system, whatever the study

may be called or whatever its goal may be.

        Even though the PBRP’s purpose was to solve load demand issues in the Permian Basin,

the addition of the 400-mile import paths required an accurate and complete system-wide model.

It would be irrational to argue that a system model lacking substantial load and generation input

could somehow properly analyze the power transfer capability from the Central Texas Corridor,

a region already in supply deficit. ERCOT’s 2023, 2024, and 2025-RTPs all state that the Central

Texas Corridor requires additional power import due to its supply deficit. 26 This alone is proof

enough that the results of the PBRP are not trustworthy, because it appears to report there is

excess power that can be transferred from the Central Texas Corridor to the Permian.

        Inspection of the questionable PBRP model inputs shows how ERCOT’s model likely

manufactured the modeled power flow from east to west. The spatial imbalance of only placing

the new HB 5066 large load demands in the Permian, while placing the offsetting generation

supply predominately in the east, created a scenario that caused or enabled the model to take

power from east to west, an otherwise seemingly impossible result that would not exist in reality.

          The Applicants argue that “The PBRP was developed in response to the Commission’s

Order in Project No. 55718, issued in December 2023, with the intention of completing the study

by July 2024. As required by House Bill 5066 (“H.B. 5066”), the load data for West Texas was

based in part on load forecast information provided by transmission service providers

practical reality of conducting a special-purpose study on ever-changing transmission topology

and a system with a large amount of load growth in a short window of time.” 28

          First, the HB 5066 load forecasts, which HB 5066 required ERCOT to consider, not in

part but in their entirety, were all available at the same time in early 2024. 29 The Applicants have

provided no evidence that ERCOT received the Permian Basin TSP load forecasts and then at

some later date received TSP load forecasts for the remainder of the State, as they seem to assert.
